title: Journalist Salary Guide: Award Rates vs National Minimum Wage
description: Understand journalist salary under the Journalists Published Media Award 2020. Compare award minimum rates to the National Minimum Wage, casual loading, super, and tax for 2026-27.

faqs.q: What is the minimum hourly rate for a journalist under the award?
faqs.a: Under the Journalists Published Media Award 2020, the minimum hourly rate ranges from $32.13 (Band 1 Level 1) to $61.12 (Band 3 Level 13) for full-time employees working 38 ordinary hours per week. These rates are set by the Fair Work Commission and are updated annually.

faqs.q: How is casual loading applied to a journalist salary?
faqs.a: Casual employees under the award receive a 25% loading on top of the ordinary hourly rate. For example, a Band 1 Level 1 casual journalist would be paid $32.13 + 25% = $40.16 per hour. The casual loading is not included when calculating overtime or penalty rates.

faqs.q: Does superannuation get paid on top of the journalist salary?
faqs.a: Yes. Under the Superannuation Guarantee, employers must contribute 12% of ordinary earnings (up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year) on top of the journalist's base salary. This is not deducted from the employee's pay.

bodyMarkdown:
## Journalist Salary: Award Rates vs the National Minimum Wage

If you're working out a **journalist salary** in Australia, the first thing to know is that most journalists are covered by the **Journalists Published Media Award 2020** (MA000067). This award sets minimum pay rates that are significantly higher than the National Minimum Wage. Understanding the difference helps you negotiate or check your pay.

### How to Convert an Hourly Rate to Annual Pay

The standard formula for annual gross pay is:

**hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For a full-time journalist under the award, ordinary hours are 38 per week. So a Band 1 Level 1 journalist earning $32.13 per hour would have:

- Weekly: $32.13 × 38 = $1,221.10
- Fortnightly: $1,221.10 × 2 = $2,442.20
- Annual: $32.13 × 38 × 52 = $63,497.68

This assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, and no penalty rates or allowances. The [pay guides](/blog) from the Fair Work Ombudsman include all minimum rates and allowances.

### National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour (or $33.05 for casuals including 25% loading). That applies to employees not covered by an award or agreement. But a journalist covered by the award must be paid at least the award rate for their classification.

Even the lowest award classification – Band 1 Level 1 – pays $32.13 per hour, which is 22% above the National Minimum Wage. Higher classifications go up to $61.12 per hour (Band 3 Level 13).

### Casual Loading for Journalists

Casual employees under the award get a 25% loading on top of the ordinary hourly rate. For example:

- Band 1 Level 1 casual: $32.13 + 25% = $40.16 per hour
- Band 2 Level 8 casual: $41.69 + 25% = $52.11 per hour

The loading compensates for not receiving paid leave. When calculating overtime or penalty rates, the casual loading is excluded – you use the base ordinary hourly rate.

### Superannuation Is Paid on Top

Under the Superannuation Guarantee, employers must contribute 12% of ordinary earnings into a super fund. This is on top of your salary, not deducted from it. For a journalist earning $63,497.68 per year, that's an extra $7,619.72 in super (up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830).

### Tax on a Journalist Salary (2026–27)

Income tax is calculated on your gross annual salary. The 2026–27 resident tax rates are:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% of excess over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: $4,020 + 30% of excess over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: $31,020 + 37% of excess over $135,000
- $190,001+: $51,370 + 45% of excess over $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (with reductions for low incomes). For a journalist earning $63,497.68, the estimated tax (including Medicare) would be around $11,000–$12,000, leaving take-home pay of about $51,500–$52,500.

Use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page for a more detailed estimate.

### Fortnightly Pay and Budgeting

Many employers pay fortnightly. For a Band 1 Level 1 journalist:

- Fortnightly gross: $2,442.20
- Fortnightly tax (approx): $420–$460
- Fortnightly net: ~$1,980–$2,020

Knowing your fortnightly amount helps with budgeting and comparing job offers.

### Why Award Rates Matter

The award also includes allowances (e.g., for working away from home, using a vehicle) and penalty rates for overtime, weekends, and public holidays. These are on top of the minimum hourly rate. The [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page explains the difference between award and national minimum.

If you're a casual journalist, remember that the casual loading is separate from penalty rates. For overtime, casuals get 150% for the first 2 hours and 200% after that (based on the ordinary hourly rate without loading).

### Summary

A journalist salary under the award starts well above the National Minimum Wage. Use the hourly rate × 38 × 52 formula to estimate annual gross, add 12% super on top, and deduct tax using the 2026–27 scale. The [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool can help you switch between hourly, weekly, and annual figures.

Always check the latest Fair Work Ombudsman pay guides for your specific classification and any allowances you're entitled to.
